extracted.intended_audience: journalists, authors, editors, students, and anyone concerned with plagiarism and writing ethics
extracted.subtask_short: avoiding plagiarism in journalism and writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on recognizing, preventing, and responding to plagiarism and fabrication in journalism and literature, with historical examples and practical prevention measures for writers and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality as a requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality isn’t just a virtue – it’s a requirement. In journalism and literature, originality is the foundation of credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain unique reporting or creative content; understand that plagiarism erodes trust, damages reputations, and can alter public discourse and cultural records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper attribution and citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Always credit sources and inspirations; give proper citation even in opinion pieces or informal sourcing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sloppy attribution mistakes. Failure to cite can lead to suspensions, retractions, or loss of publishing contracts (examples: Fareed Zakaria, Maureen Dowd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking and source verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigorous fact-checking and verification of quotes, scenes, and reported details are essential to ethical journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial practices should include fact-checking and mentorship structures; weak oversight enables fabrication and plagiarism (example: Jayson Blair, overhaul of NYT practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fabricate
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabrication—making up quotes, sources, or events—is a grave ethical violation distinct from but related to plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrication can lead to retractions and revoked awards (example: Janet Cooke's Pulitzer was revoked). Avoid composite characters or invented scenes presented as factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid copying passages, quotes, or plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not copy quotes, passages, plots, character descriptions, or story ideas from other works without clear permission and attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In journalism this includes lifting story ideas or passages; in literature this includes copying plots or character material (examples: Kaavya Viswanathan, Alex Haley, Q.R. Markham). Publishers may recall books and cancel contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge influences; avoid 'unconscious borrowing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers must acknowledge influences and avoid relying on claims of 'unconscious' borrowing as a defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When similarities arise, transparently credit inspirations or resolve disputes; legal settlements and reputational damage can follow unchecked borrowing (example: Alex Haley settled after Courlander suit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plagiarism detection tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ plagiarism detection tools (OriginalityReport, Grammarly, Turnitin, Copyscape, etc.) as part of the editorial workflow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools can catch unattributed borrowings but are not foolproof; combine automated checks with editorial judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep detailed notes and citations during research
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain organized research notes and citations to ensure accurate attribution and to defend sourcing decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good note-taking reduces accidental omission of credits and helps editors verify provenance of material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand fair use and copyright laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers and editors should be familiar with fair use doctrine and copyright rules relevant to their jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal understanding helps distinguish permissible reuse from copyright infringement and prevents legal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice ethical writing habits and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate habits of transparency about sources, methods, and contributions (including use of assistants or AI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency builds trust; disclose ghostwriters, significant editorial interventions, or AI assistance when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial enforcement and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and publishers must enforce rigorous standards and provide training on attribution, sourcing, and ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional checks—policies, mentorship, and enforcement—reduce risk of scandals and systemic failures (NYT overhaul after Blair).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overrely on research assistants or ghostwriters
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overreliance on others for content without vetting and proper attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ghostwritten or assistant-produced material must be checked; failure to supervise can lead to unattributed borrowings in memoirs and political books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed cannot replace accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Deadline pressure is a common cause of plagiarism and fabrication; prioritize accuracy over speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should resist incentives that reward speed over verification; rushing leads to careless attribution and factual errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for AI-generated content and 'invisible' plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-generated content can reproduce existing text and create 'invisible' plagiarism; publishers/authors are responsible for checking AI outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review and fact-check AI drafts, use detection where possible, and be aware of recent retractions for AI-assisted stories (example: CNET).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid recycling material without credit (including self-plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reusing previously published material without disclosure or credit is an unethical form of recycling content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose prior publication or reuse to editors/readers; treat recycled material transparently to avoid accusations of duplicate publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and corrective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared for and enact appropriate corrective actions—retractions, corrections, suspensions, firing, returned prizes, and legal settlements—when misconduct occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Swift, transparent remedies help restore trust; examples include resignations, revoked awards, public corrections, and legal settlements (Blair, Cooke, Goodwin, Haley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish inspiration/homage from theft
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the blurry line between intertextuality, homage, and plagiarism and make clear acknowledgments when drawing on other works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using allusion or intertextual techniques, explicitly credit sources or frame material as homage to avoid accusations (example: debates around Helene Hegemann and Stig Sæterbakken).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deceptive online behavior (e.g., pseudonymous attacks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use pseudonyms or deceptive online personas to attack critics or mask misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such behavior compounds ethical breaches and damages credibility (example: Johann Hari's use of pseudonyms and subsequent fallout).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent idea theft—don't lift story ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect ownership of reporting ideas and beats; avoid appropriating others' story concepts without credit or collaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribution of unique scoops or concepts and clear boundaries between inspiration and appropriation reduce disputes.
